The orange lamps are sodium-vapour discharge lamps, which contain sodium vapour plus neon/argon starting gas. The supporting phenomenon is kept (street-light colours, an inert gas that does not react) but made accurate. records.old: with the blue-white glow of newer xenon/argon-filled LED street lights prompt the question: why do different group I and VIII elements emit completely different colours of light, and why is argon (a noble gas) useful precisely because it does NOT react with the hot metal filament?
records.new: with the white glow of newer LED street lights (which contain no gas at all) prompt the question: why does sodium vapour glow orange, and why do sodium-vapour lamps also contain neon and argon, noble gases that do NOT react with the hot sodium vapour?

records.why: Teachers had no description of what students are likely to write or of what a good prediction sounds like. Added the common ideas (these match the two misconceptions already named in the Formative Assessment) and a model of a strong prediction.
records.old: Do not correct any prediction. Close by saying
records.new: Do not correct any prediction. WHAT TO EXPECT: many students will write that sodium will 'do nothing' or 'dissolve' because it is 'in salt', that magnesium will react the same way 'because both are metals', that argon will react because 'it is next to chlorine', and (prompt 4) that potassium is less reactive than sodium because it is 'heavier' or that lithium is more reactive because it is 'lighter'. A strong prediction says that pure sodium reacts violently, magnesium less, argon not at all, potassium more and lithium less than sodium, with a reason based on position or electrons. records.why: The teacher had no answer key for the observation table. Added the expected observations and an example of a good versus a weak inference.
records.old: Collect one Observation Table per group at the end of the lesson for review.
records.new: Collect one Observation Table per group at the end of the lesson for review. EXPECTED OBSERVATIONS (what good looks like): sodium floats and skims, fizzes, burns with an orange flame, the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein, and a gas is made; magnesium gives a few tiny bubbles and no flame, at most a faint pink; aluminium shows no visible change; argon: nothing happens. A good inference is 'a gas is produced and the water has become alkaline'; a weak one only repeats the observation ('it fizzed').

records.why: The text had every group receive its own rice-grain piece of lithium and sodium, placed by the teacher in each group trough. That contradicts the safety note (teacher only, behind a screen), the overview (teacher demonstrates) and is unworkable with large classes (10 or more troughs, the teacher cutting and placing metal at each). All three metals are now teacher demonstrations; students still collect the data. The teacher must confirm this fits their class size and screens.
records.old: STAGE 1 — Lithium with water (student-conducted with teacher at the front): Each group receives a large clear plastic trough half-filled with distilled water, a small piece of universal indicator paper (or 3 drops of universal indicator solution added to the water), and a test tube for gas collection. The teacher uses tongs to place a rice-grain piece of lithium into each group trough. Students observe and record: speed of reaction, appearance of the metal surface, sound, whether the metal sinks or floats, gas produced (test tube inverted over metal to collect gas — teacher brings a lighted splint to each group for testing), and colour change of indicator. STAGE 2 — Sodium with water (student-conducted, repeating Lesson 1 observations now with data collection): Teacher provides each group with a rice-grain piece of sodium. Students repeat observations and gas test, and measure pH using the indicator.
records.new: STAGE 1 — Lithium with water (TEACHER DEMONSTRATION at the front bench, behind a safety screen; students stay in their groups at least 1.5 metres away): The teacher uses tongs to place a rice-grain piece of lithium on the water in a large clear plastic trough (3 drops of universal indicator in the water) and holds an inverted test tube over the reacting metal to collect gas, then tests it once with a lighted splint for the whole class. Students observe and record: speed of reaction, appearance of the metal surface, sound, whether the metal sinks or floats, gas produced, splint result and colour change of the indicator. STAGE 2 — Sodium with water (TEACHER DEMONSTRATION, same set-up in a fresh trough, repeating Lesson 1 but now with data collection): the teacher adds a rice-grain piece of sodium; students repeat the observations and record the indicator colour.

records.why: LiOH, NaOH and KOH are all strong bases that dissociate in water, so equal amounts in equal water give about the same pH; a 'highest pH for potassium' result is not reliable and 'pH 8' is too low for a strong alkali. Checked: 0.01 mol/L of a strong base is pH 12.
records.old: All three produced alkaline solutions (pH 8 to 14), with potassium producing the highest pH reading.
records.new: All three produced strongly alkaline solutions (universal indicator blue-purple, roughly pH 11 to 14); the readings are similar because LiOH, NaOH and KOH are all strong alkalis, so the exact pH depends on how much metal and water are used, not on which metal.
records.reference: Brown, LeMay, Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science, chapters on periodic properties of the elements and on nonmetals/metals

records.why: The analogy was used with no statement of where it breaks down. Limits added. Checked: Mg first and second ionisation energies are 738 and 1451 kJ/mol.
records.old: WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before cold-calling 2 students who had incorrect predictions.
records.new: WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before cold-calling 2 students who had incorrect predictions. LIMITS OF THE 'TWO-ELECTRON TAX' (say this aloud before leaving the frame): a tax is paid away and gone, but the electrons are not lost, they move to the other reactant (here the oxygen in water) and the energy released when the new compounds form helps repay the cost; the real cost also has two parts, because the second electron costs more than the first (Mg: 738 then 1451 kJ/mol), so the first ionisation energy alone is only a simple guide; and magnesium's slow reaction in cold water is partly because a coat of Mg(OH)2/MgO sticks to the ribbon.

records.value:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your professional journal:

1. CONCEPTUAL DEPTH — Did students reach a causal explanation (ionisation energy / nuclear charge / shielding) or did they stay at the descriptive level ('magnesium reacts more slowly')? Which groups needed the most prompting to move from description to mechanism? What question or prompt worked best to push them deeper?

2. PRACTICAL MANAGEMENT — How well did Investigation A (magnesium in cold water) work in practice? If bubbles were too slow to observe meaningfully, note whether pre-cleaning the ribbon with sandpaper was sufficient, or whether a longer observation window is needed. Were groups able to collect enough gas over cold water for a reliable splint test?

3. ANCHORING PHENOMENON CONNECTION — Did students spontaneously reference the Kisumu sodium explosion as a comparison benchmark, or did they need teacher prompting to make that connection? If prompting was always needed, consider making the comparison more structurally explicit in the worksheet (e.g., a column headed 'How does this compare to sodium in Kisumu?').

4. DQB QUALITY — Were the orange (wonder) notes genuine new questions raised by today's evidence, or recycled questions from Lessons 1–2? If recycled, this suggests students do not yet see today's evidence as generating new puzzles — consider spending an extra 2 minutes in Phase 4 modelling what a genuinely new question looks like.

5. EQUITY CHECK — Which students were cold-called today? Review your clipboard notes: were the same students called repeatedly? Identify 2–3 students who have not yet spoken aloud in plenary and plan specific cold-call moments for them in Lesson 4.

6. MODEL COMPLETENESS — Are students' cumulative diagrams building coherently across lessons, or are they becoming cluttered and hard to read? If the latter, consider providing a clean A3 template for Lesson 4 that students can use to re-draw their model with all updates to date incorporated neatly.

records.why: Cyclohexane (used in the displacement demonstrations) and chlorine exposure for asthmatic learners were not covered by the safety note.
records.old: Have sodium thiosulfate solution available to neutralise any spillage.
records.new: Have sodium thiosulfate solution available to neutralise any spillage. Cyclohexane is flammable and harmful: keep it away from flames and use no more than 1 cm³ per test. Learners with asthma or breathing difficulties sit at the back, away from the chlorine demonstration (or watch a video clip instead).

records.why: Iron wool does not react with chlorine gas on its own at room temperature (it must be heated) and chlorine gas must only be made in a fume cupboard; the old text also called it 'chlorine water' in the heading but a gas jar in the body. The teacher must decide whether the school has a fume cupboard and a safe chlorine source, or should use a video.
records.old: Demo 2 — Chlorine water + iron wool: Iron wool is placed in a gas jar of chlorine; learners observe brown iron(III) chloride forming.
records.new: Demo 2 — Chlorine + iron wool: heated iron wool is lowered into a gas jar of chlorine by the teacher in a fume cupboard; learners observe brown iron(III) chloride forming. records.why: The old text said aluminium and silicon do not react 'because of higher effective nuclear charge', with the oxide layer only in brackets. The oxide layer is the main reason aluminium shows no reaction with cold water. Recomputed twice: Al IE1 + IE2 + IE3 = 578 + 1817 + 2745 = 5140 kJ/mol; Mg IE1 + IE2 = 738 + 1451 = 2189; Na 496.
records.old: aluminium and silicon have even higher effective nuclear charges and more outer electrons to remove (Al first ionisation energy, 577 kJ per mole, dips below Mg at 738 because its single 3p electron is easier to remove, but the total energy to remove all three outer electrons is much higher, and Al is also protected by its oxide layer), so they do not react with cold water at all; the anchoring phenomenon is now fully explained by the left-to-right increase in effective nuclear charge across period 3.
records.new: aluminium has an even higher effective nuclear charge and three outer electrons to remove (its first ionisation energy, 578 kJ per mole, dips below Mg at 738 because its single 3p electron is easier to remove, but the total energy to remove all three outer electrons, about 5140 kJ per mole, is far higher than for sodium's one, 496), and above all it is protected by a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide that keeps water away from the metal, so it shows no reaction with cold water; silicon is a non-metal with a giant covalent structure that does not give up electrons, so it does not react either; the anchoring phenomenon is now explained for the metals by the left-to-right increase in effective nuclear charge across period 3, with aluminium's oxide layer as the second factor.
records.reference: Brown, LeMay, Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science, chapters on periodic properties of the elements and on nonmetals/metals; NIST Atomic Spectra Database, ionisation energies of Na, Mg, Al

records.why: Audit item verified as a real problem: the exemplar blamed only nuclear charge and the number of electrons, and never named the oxide layer that the prompt asks students to suggest. Recomputed: Al 578 + 1817 + 2745 = 5140 kJ/mol.

value.criterion: Use of electron configuration and position
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: correctly writes electron configurations and clearly links group and period to outer electrons and shells in every part.

value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains most trends with two of the key ideas, with some imprecision.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: describes trends without a causal explanation, or uses ideas incorrectly.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: cites specific observations and values (such as 496, 738, 578 and 1521 kJ/mol, lilac flame, kanga bleaching) accurately and consistently.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: cites some evidence accurately, though not always specifically.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: little or no evidence is cited, or the evidence is inaccurate.

value.developing: Approaches Expectations: prediction or application is missing or unjustified, with no clear link back to the phenomenon.

records.why: The partner contract allows only three rubric level fields, so the fourth CBE level, Below Expectations, cannot be represented in the current Final Explanation. Suggestion: if the contract can add a fourth level, use 'Below Expectations: little or no relevant explanation, with major errors'. Until then teachers can add it by hand.

KICD content that is not taught or assessed in the 7 lessons: (1) size of IONS (ionic radius) and of atoms across groups beyond Group I/II/VII; (2) electron affinity across Period 3; (3) boiling points across Period 3 and down Groups I, II and VII (only melting points are graphed); (4) Group I and II metals reacting with oxygen and chlorine (only Mg with oxygen is written as an equation, nothing is demonstrated); (5) Group II with dilute acids other than Mg; (6) period 3 elements reacting with chlorine, with alkalis and with hydrogen; (7) preparing chlorine gas. Concrete suggestions: in Lesson 5 Activity B have Group C plot boiling point on the same sheet as melting point and Group D plot electron affinity (a data card is needed); give Lesson 6 a one-page data card on the reactions of Na, Mg, Al, Si, S with oxygen and chlorine (no demonstration, because of time and chlorine hazards); add ionic radius to the Lesson 5 data table. Teachers must decide what the 12 periods can hold; KICD itself suggests 34 lessons for this sub-strand.

Numbering and names checked against the KICD March 2025 Chemistry design: sub-strand 1.5 Periodicity is correct. The unit names Strand 1.0 as 'Chemical Families' but KICD names Strand 1.0 'Inorganic Chemistry' ('chemical families' appears only in the key inquiry question and the value text). The strand name was not changed. KICD suggests 34 lessons for the sub-strand; this sequence has 7 lessons (12 periods). The KICD learning outcomes (a to e), key inquiry questions and content bullets in the data already match the KICD text.

The anchoring phenomenon, Summary and Final Explanation name 'the Kisumu Water and Sanitation Company'. The Kisumu utility is usually named the Kisumu Water and Sewerage Company (KIWASCO), and the careers text names the 'Nairobi Water and Sewerage Company' (the current name is Nairobi City Water and Sewerage Company). Because the phenomenon is a demonstration that real staff would not normally run, suggest naming 'a water treatment plant in Kisumu' instead of a real company. Not changed here because the name appears in every lesson; Kenyan teachers should confirm the correct name and decide.
